questions.stem: An observational study links coffee drinking to lung cancer. Smoking is more common among coffee drinkers, independently causes lung cancer and is not caused by coffee drinking. Which problem does adjustment for smoking aim to reduce?
options: Selection bias
Reverse causation
Confounding
Observer bias
Recall bias
questions.why: Smoking is a **confounder** because it is associated with the exposure and independently influences the outcome without being an intermediate on the proposed pathway.
distractors: This concerns how entry or retention creates a distorted comparison, not the specified third-variable pathway.
This would mean the outcome influences the exposure, rather than the stated third factor explaining part of the association.
This concerns systematic differences in assessment or recording.
This concerns differences in remembering past exposure.
lo: Define epidemiology and describe the main components of an observational study
sources: Cochrane Handbook: Risk of bias in a randomised trial — https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-08
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Heart Failure).

keyClues.quote: Smoking is more common among coffee drinkers
explanation: Smoking is associated with the exposure being studied; this is one necessary feature of the proposed confounder.
Smoking also affects the outcome, giving a non-coffee explanation for part of the observed association.

keyClues.quote: is not caused by coffee drinking
explanation: This keeps smoking off the proposed causal pathway from coffee to cancer. Adjustment addresses a confounder here, not a problem of recall or outcome observation.

keyConcept.summary: Smoking is a confounder because it is associated with the exposure and independently influences the outcome without being an intermediate on the proposed pathway.
paragraphs: Adjustment can reduce measured confounding, but residual or unmeasured confounding may remain. An adjusted association is therefore not automatically proof of causation. Always draw the proposed exposure–factor–outcome relationships before naming the problem.

commonTraps: A variable associated with both exposure and outcome is not always a confounder if it lies on the causal pathway.
recogniseNextTime: This helps distinguish a confounder from a mediator.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Would adjusting for a mediator estimate the same total effect?
followUpQuestions.answer: No; it can remove part of the effect being studied.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Smoking is a confounder because it is associated with the exposure and independently influences the outcome without being an intermediate on the proposed pathway.

questions.stem: An ECG shows regular P waves at 80/min and regular QRS complexes at 35/min, with changing PR intervals and no consistent relationship between atrial and ventricular activity. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Mobitz I second-degree AV block
Complete heart block
Mobitz II second-degree AV block
First-degree AV block
Sinus bradycardia
questions.why: The atria and ventricles are beating independently: **AV dissociation with a slow escape rhythm** is consistent with complete heart block.
distractors: PR intervals progressively lengthen before a dropped QRS, rather than persistent independent rhythms.
Intermittent P waves fail to conduct, but conducted beats retain a relationship to their P waves.
Every P wave conducts with a prolonged but fixed PR interval.
The slow sinus rate would still produce a consistent P–QRS relationship.
lo: Identify the ECG features of common tachy- and brady-arrhythmias (i.e. atrial fibrillation/flutter, ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation and heart block)
sources: Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Heart Failure).

keyClues.quote: P waves at 80/min and regular QRS complexes at 35/min
explanation: Atrial activity and a slower ventricular escape rhythm coexist. The atrial rate is not simply a slow sinus rate.

keyClues.quote: no consistent relationship between atrial and ventricular activity
explanation: Complete AV dissociation supports third-degree block. First-degree and second-degree blocks preserve conduction of at least some atrial impulses.

keyConcept.summary: The atria and ventricles are beating independently: AV dissociation with a slow escape rhythm is consistent with complete heart block.
paragraphs: A ventricular escape rhythm can maintain some output when atrial impulses do not reach the ventricles. Identify atrial rate, ventricular rate and their relationship separately; a slow rate alone is insufficient to classify the block.

commonTraps: Not every bradycardia is sinus bradycardia.
recogniseNextTime: The absence of atrioventricular linkage distinguishes complete block from delayed or intermittently failed conduction.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What happens to the PR interval in first-degree AV block?
followUpQuestions.answer: It is prolonged but consistent, with every P wave followed by a QRS.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: The atria and ventricles are beating independently: AV dissociation with a slow escape rhythm is consistent with complete heart block.

questions.stem: A chest X-ray report describes consolidation that obscures the right heart border while the right hemidiaphragm remains visible. Which lobe is most likely involved?
options: Left upper lobe
Right upper lobe
Right lower lobe
Right middle lobe
Left lower lobe
questions.why: The **right middle lobe** lies adjacent to the right heart border. Consolidation removes the normal air–soft-tissue contrast at that interface.
distractors: Its lingula lies against the left, rather than right, heart border.
This does not normally contact the right heart border in the same way.
Lower-lobe disease more characteristically obscures the right hemidiaphragm.
This is associated with the left hemidiaphragm and retrocardiac region.
lo: Use a systematic method to review a chest x-ray of a patient with respiratory symptoms.
sources: Clinical Methods: Chest roentgenography for pulmonary evaluation — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK370/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Introduction).

explanation: The right middle lobe contacts this border, so loss of the silhouette localises adjacent consolidation there.
Preservation of that interface makes right lower-lobe consolidation less likely as the cause of the described silhouette loss.

keyConcept.summary: The right middle lobe lies adjacent to the right heart border
paragraphs: The silhouette sign localises disease by identifying which normal border disappears. It depends on contact between structures of similar radiographic density. This question uses a written report, so no unseen image is required.

commonTraps: Do not use “right-sided shadowing” alone to assign a lobe.
recogniseNextTime: A preserved diaphragm helps distinguish middle- from lower-lobe disease.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which region commonly obscures the left heart border?
followUpQuestions.answer: The lingula of the left upper lobe.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: The right middle lobe lies adjacent to the right heart border

questions.stem: A screening programme detects a disproportionately high share of slow-growing cancers because they remain detectable without symptoms for longer. Screen-detected patients consequently have better survival even before treatment effects are considered. Which bias is this?
options: Length-time bias
Recall bias
Verification bias
Attrition bias
Lead-time bias
questions.why: **Length-time bias** occurs because periodic screening is more likely to encounter disease with a long detectable preclinical phase.
distractors: This concerns recollection of previous exposures.
This arises when the reference test is applied differently according to initial test results.
This concerns missing follow-up and does not explain preferential detection of slow-growing lesions.
This increases measured survival by moving diagnosis earlier, even for the same disease course.
lo: Explain the principles of screening and provide an overview of all of the UK screening programme
sources: What Cancer Screening Statistics Really Tell Us - NCI — https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/screening/research/what-screening-statistics-mean
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Start in Life.

explanation: Screening preferentially samples cancers with a longer detectable preclinical phase; this is selection by disease natural history.

keyClues.quote: remain detectable without symptoms for longer
explanation: The key is a longer detection window, not simply moving the date of diagnosis earlier in an otherwise unchanged disease course. The latter is lead-time bias.

keyConcept.summary: Length-time bias occurs because periodic screening is more likely to encounter disease with a long detectable preclinical phase.
paragraphs: A screened group can appear to fare better because of the types of tumour detected. Mortality outcomes and appropriate comparison groups are needed to judge benefit; survival after diagnosis alone is insufficient.

commonTraps: Lead time and length time both affect screening interpretation, but through different mechanisms.
recogniseNextTime: The cases selected have a different natural history; this is not merely a change in the start date of the survival clock.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What would unchanged age at death despite earlier diagnosis suggest?
followUpQuestions.answer: Lead-time bias.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Length-time bias occurs because periodic screening is more likely to encounter disease with a long detectable preclinical phase.

questions.stem: A patient has exertional calf pain that resolves with rest and a cool foot with an absent dorsalis pedis pulse. Which additional finding would support chronic arterial insufficiency?
options: Brown pigmentation around the medial ankle
Bilateral pitting ankle oedema with preserved pulses
Prominent superficial varicose veins
Pallor on elevation with dependent rubor
A shallow exuding ulcer above the medial malleolus
questions.why: **Elevation pallor and dependent rubor** support impaired arterial perfusion alongside claudication and reduced pulses.
distractors: Gaiter-zone pigmentation favours chronic venous hypertension.
This is more consistent with venous or systemic fluid accumulation.
Varicosities indicate superficial venous disease rather than impaired arterial inflow.
This distribution and appearance favour a venous ulcer.
questions.module: Circulation (Peripheral Arterial Disease & Venous Thromboembolic Disease)
lo: Carry out a physical examination of the peripheral arteries or veins, appropriate to the patient's symptoms
sources: 2024 ACC/AHA/AACVPR/APMA/ABC/SCAI/SVM/SVN/SVS/SIR/VESS Guideline for the Management of Lower Extremity Peripheral Artery Disease - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12728805/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Circulation (Peripheral Arterial Disease & Venous Thromboembolic Disease).

keyClues.quote: exertional calf pain that resolves with rest
explanation: Reproducible exercise-related pain relieved by rest is typical of intermittent claudication.

keyClues.quote: a cool foot with an absent dorsalis pedis pulse
explanation: Poor arterial delivery fits elevation pallor and dependent rubor. Varicosities, medial ankle pigmentation and a venous-pattern ulcer support venous disease instead.

keyConcept.summary: Elevation pallor and dependent rubor support impaired arterial perfusion alongside claudication and reduced pulses.
paragraphs: Arterial disease limits delivery of oxygenated blood. Venous disease impairs drainage and commonly produces oedema and gaiter skin changes. These processes can coexist, so one finding should not replace a vascular examination.

commonTraps: A lower-leg ulcer is not automatically arterial; location, appearance and pulses matter.
recogniseNextTime: A reproducible exertional demand–supply mismatch supports claudication.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What bedside pressure comparison helps assess arterial perfusion?
followUpQuestions.answer: The ankle–brachial pressure index, interpreted with awareness of non-compressible arteries.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.stem: A prespecified trial analysis gives a two-sided p value of 0.02. Which interpretation is correct under the test’s assumptions?
options: The probability that the null hypothesis is true is 0.02
If the null hypothesis were true, results at least this extreme would occur with probability 0.02
The estimated treatment effect is wrong in 2% of patients
The probability that the treatment is clinically useful is 0.98
The chance that another trial will find significance is 0.98
questions.why: A p value describes **the extremeness of the data under the null model**; it does not assign a probability to the hypothesis being true.
distractors: A p value is conditional on the null, not the probability of the null itself.
The p value is not an individual-level error rate.
Statistical evidence does not directly give clinical usefulness or its probability.
Replication depends on effect size, design and sampling variation.
lo: Explain the basic framework for statistical hypothesis testing (such as p-values,confidence intervals etc.)
sources: Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Infections).

explanation: The interpretation depends on the statistical model and analysis being appropriate.

keyConcept.summary: A p value describes the extremeness of the data under the null model; it does not assign a probability to the hypothesis being true.
paragraphs: Effect size and its uncertainty are needed alongside the p value. A small but precisely estimated difference may have little clinical importance, whereas an uncertain estimate can still include important benefits and harms.

commonTraps: Do not translate p = 0.02 into “98% chance the treatment works”.
recogniseNextTime: The interpretation depends on the statistical model and analysis being appropriate.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What helps assess the size and precision of the effect?
followUpQuestions.answer: The effect estimate and confidence interval.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: A p value describes the extremeness of the data under the null model; it does not assign a probability to the hypothesis being true.

questions.stem: A patient with resistant hypertension and widespread atherosclerosis has a marked creatinine rise soon after an ACE inhibitor is started. They are euvolaemic, take no NSAIDs and have no urinary obstruction. Which underlying condition best explains this response?
options: Uncomplicated essential hypertension
Isolated unilateral renal artery stenosis with a healthy opposite kidney
Bilateral renal artery stenosis
Phaeochromocytoma
Primary hyperaldosteronism
questions.why: In **bilateral renal artery stenosis**, filtration may depend on angiotensin II-mediated efferent constriction. ACE inhibition removes that support and can markedly reduce GFR.
distractors: A marked rise requires investigation rather than attribution to uncomplicated hypertension.
The opposite kidney can often preserve overall filtration, making a large global decline less likely.
Catecholamine excess causes hypertension but does not specifically explain this renal haemodynamic response.
This explains some resistant hypertension but not the characteristic dependence of filtration on angiotensin II.
lo: Identify the risk factors predisposing to high blood pressure, including the causes of secondary hypertension
sources: Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Circulation (Hypertension).

explanation: This raises the prior likelihood of atherosclerotic renal artery disease.

keyClues.quote: marked creatinine rise soon after an ACE inhibitor
explanation: When renal perfusion is severely limited, angiotensin-II-mediated efferent tone may sustain filtration. Removing it can cause a substantial fall in GFR.

keyClues.quote: euvolaemic, take no NSAIDs and have no urinary obstruction
explanation: The stem removes common competing explanations for an acute fall in filtration after treatment. A healthy opposite kidney often preserves overall filtration with unilateral disease, making bilateral disease the best fit here.

keyConcept.summary: In bilateral renal artery stenosis, filtration may depend on angiotensin II-mediated efferent constriction
paragraphs: Reduced inflow pressure activates the renin–angiotensin system. Efferent arteriolar tone helps maintain glomerular pressure despite impaired inflow. A creatinine rise is a clue requiring assessment, not proof of stenosis by itself.

commonTraps: Do not equate every small creatinine rise after ACE inhibition with bilateral stenosis.
recogniseNextTime: These details reduce competing explanations for an ACE inhibitor-associated fall in filtration.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which arteriole is directly affected by the loss of angiotensin II support?
followUpQuestions.answer: The efferent arteriole dilates.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: In bilateral renal artery stenosis, filtration may depend on angiotensin II-mediated efferent constriction

questions.stem: A hypothetical drug is given by continuous intravenous infusion. Clearance is 5 L/hour and the target steady-state concentration is 4 mg/L. Assuming linear kinetics, what maintenance infusion rate is required?
options: 1.25 mg/hour
20 mg/hour
25 mg/hour
9 mg/hour
80 mg/hour
questions.why: At steady state, input equals elimination: **rate = clearance × concentration** = 5 × 4 = 20 mg/hour.
distractors: Dividing clearance by concentration gives the wrong dimensions.
This is not the product of the supplied clearance and concentration.
Adding values with different units does not calculate a dose rate.
This is four times the required rate.
lo: Calculate drug dilutions and doses using volumes of distribution and drug clearances to obtain safe and effective concentrations of drugs in plasma
sources: Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Introductory Week.

explanation: At steady state, input equals elimination; this asks for a maintenance rate rather than a loading dose.
Clearance must multiply the target concentration so that litres cancel, leaving mass per time.
The calculation is 5 L/hour × 4 mg/L = 20 mg/hour. Squaring or otherwise rescaling either supplied value is not part of this relationship.

keyConcept.summary: At steady state, input equals elimination: rate = clearance × concentration = 5 × 4 = 20 mg/hour.
paragraphs: Maintenance dosing replaces the amount eliminated over time. It is distinct from a loading dose, which depends on distribution volume and establishes the initial concentration. The numerical example is hypothetical, not a prescribing instruction.

commonTraps: Do not use volume of distribution in place of clearance for a maintenance rate.
recogniseNextTime: Intravenous delivery means bioavailability is one, so no oral correction is needed.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If clearance halves with the target unchanged, what rate is needed?
followUpQuestions.answer: 10 mg/hour.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: At steady state, input equals elimination: rate = clearance × concentration = 5 × 4 = 20 mg/hour.

questions.stem: A standard blood-pressure cuff is used on an arm larger than the cuff’s stated size range. Which systematic error is most likely?
options: Systolic is overestimated while diastolic is underestimated
Both systolic and diastolic readings are overestimated
Both systolic and diastolic readings are underestimated
Systolic is underestimated while diastolic is overestimated
Pulse pressure is abolished despite a readable mean pressure
questions.why: An **undersized cuff** generally requires excessive pressure to compress the artery adequately and can overestimate blood pressure.
distractors: The usual problem is upward bias in both readings.
An undersized cuff generally biases readings upwards, not downwards.
This mixed direction is not the usual undersized-cuff effect.
An incorrectly sized cuff does not specifically remove the arterial pulse pressure.
lo: Take a blood pressure measurement with both an electronic and an aneroid sphygmomanometer, identifying factors which may lead to inaccurate measurement
sources: Measurement of Blood Pressure in Humans: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11409525/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Circulation (Hypertension).

keyClues.quote: larger than the cuff’s stated size range
explanation: Cuff size should be chosen for arm circumference, rather than using the same cuff for everyone.

keyConcept.summary: An undersized cuff generally requires excessive pressure to compress the artery adequately and can overestimate blood pressure.
paragraphs: Before interpreting a reading, check cuff fit, arm support, position and rest. Repeating a measurement with the same wrong cuff may reproduce the same bias; repeated measurements do not automatically remove a systematic error.

commonTraps: Precision from repeated readings is different from accuracy.
recogniseNextTime: Cuff size should be chosen for arm circumference, rather than using the same cuff for everyone.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What is the first correction?
followUpQuestions.answer: Repeat measurement using an appropriately sized cuff and standard technique.

questions.stem: Two solutions have the same measured osmolality. One contains mainly a solute that rapidly crosses the cell membrane; the other contains a non-penetrating solute. Which feature best predicts their different effects on cell volume at equilibrium?
options: Total number of dissolved particles regardless of permeability
Molecular mass of the solute alone
Concentration of effective non-penetrating osmoles
Its hydrogen ion concentration alone
The solution’s total volume alone
questions.why: **Tonicity depends on effective non-penetrating solutes**. A penetrating solute may raise measured osmolality without sustaining the same transmembrane water shift.
distractors: This determines osmolality but does not fully determine sustained cell-volume effects.
Particle number and permeability matter more directly than mass alone.
pH does not define tonicity.
Volume does not specify its effective osmotic concentration.
lo: Explain the concepts of osmolarity, osmolality and tonicity
sources: Osmolality and Tonicity of Isotonic Beverages - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11120308/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Introductory Week.

explanation: Total solute particle concentration alone cannot explain why the two solutions have different sustained effects.
A penetrating solute equilibrates across the membrane and cannot sustain the same osmotic gradient as an impermeant solute.
Effective impermeant osmoles determine tonicity and the sustained direction of water movement; molecular mass or pH alone does not.

keyConcept.summary: Tonicity depends on effective non-penetrating solutes
paragraphs: Osmolality counts particles per kilogram of solvent. Tonicity predicts cell-volume change for a particular membrane. Permeability therefore matters: a short-lived osmotic effect can differ from the eventual equilibrium response.

commonTraps: Do not treat iso-osmotic and isotonic as interchangeable.
recogniseNextTime: The question asks about the sustained effect after a penetrating solute has redistributed.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Can a hyperosmotic solution fail to be hypertonic?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes, if the added osmoles readily enter the cells.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Tonicity depends on effective non-penetrating solutes

questions.stem: A patient has palpitations. The ECG shows an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm without discrete P waves. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Atrial flutter with fixed 2:1 conduction
First-degree AV block
Complete heart block
Atrial fibrillation
Sinus arrhythmia
questions.why: An **irregularly irregular rhythm without discrete P waves** is characteristic of atrial fibrillation.
distractors: This usually produces organised flutter activity and a regular ventricular response.
This retains a consistent P–QRS relationship with a prolonged PR interval.
This produces independent atrial and ventricular rhythms rather than absent organised P waves with this irregular pattern.
This retains identifiable sinus P waves before QRS complexes.
lo: Identify the ECG features of common tachy- and brady-arrhythmias (i.e. atrial fibrillation/flutter, ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation and heart block)
sources: Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Heart Failure).

explanation: Unpredictable R–R intervals fit AF and weigh against flutter with fixed conduction or a regular escape rhythm.
Organised sinus atrial activity is absent, unlike sinus arrhythmia or first-degree AV block.

keyConcept.summary: An irregularly irregular rhythm without discrete P waves is characteristic of atrial fibrillation.
paragraphs: Irregularity alone has several causes, including ectopic beats. The absence of organised P waves adds the key distinguishing feature. A rate description should therefore be paired with inspection of atrial activity.

commonTraps: Do not diagnose AF solely because the pulse is fast.
recogniseNextTime: Assess atrial activity as well as ventricular regularity.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Can AF have a slow ventricular response?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes; ventricular rate depends on AV conduction and other factors, including medicines.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: An irregularly irregular rhythm without discrete P waves is characteristic of atrial fibrillation.

questions.stem: An adult with capacity refuses a recommended transfusion after discussing the material risks, alternatives and likely consequences. They remain calm and consistent, with no evidence of pressure from others. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Seek a second capacity assessment solely because the refusal is high risk
Document the informed refusal and agree acceptable ongoing care
Ask relatives to consent on the patient’s behalf
Pause all other treatment until the patient accepts transfusion
Repeat the consent discussion until the patient changes their decision
questions.why: A capacitous adult’s **informed, voluntary refusal** should be respected, documented and incorporated into the ongoing plan.
distractors: Disagreement with a medical recommendation is not itself evidence of incapacity.
Relatives cannot override this capacitous adult’s decision.
Other acceptable care should continue; consent is specific to the intervention.
Clarification is appropriate when needed, but repeated pressure is not respect for an informed refusal.
lo: Explore different approaches to working through ethical dilemmas in medicine
sources: Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Seriously Injured Patient.

explanation: The decision belongs to the patient. Risk alone does not invalidate capacity or transfer consent to relatives.

keyClues.quote: discussing the material risks, alternatives and likely consequences
explanation: The refusal is informed; the next step is documentation and an acceptable ongoing plan.

keyClues.quote: no evidence of pressure from others
explanation: The choice is described as voluntary. Repeating persuasion until agreement or withholding other care would fail to respect that decision.

keyConcept.summary: A capacitous adult’s informed, voluntary refusal should be respected, documented and incorporated into the ongoing plan.
paragraphs: Refusal of one intervention is not refusal of every aspect of care. Clarify what remains acceptable and explain that the patient can revisit the decision. The appropriate response protects autonomy while maintaining a therapeutic relationship.

commonTraps: A decision’s riskiness is not a capacity test.
recogniseNextTime: Capacity, information and voluntariness have been addressed in the scenario.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Can the patient later change their mind?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes; consent and refusal can be revisited.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: A capacitous adult’s informed, voluntary refusal should be respected, documented and incorporated into the ongoing plan.

questions.stem: After being told that their cancer has spread, a patient becomes silent and tearful. The clinician has not yet discussed treatment options. What is the best immediate response?
options: Arrange the next appointment before continuing the conversation
Begin a detailed comparison of treatment regimens
Summarise the information again in simpler words immediately
Ask the relative present to explain what the patient is feeling
Allow a pause, acknowledge the distress and invite the patient’s response
questions.why: The immediate task is to **acknowledge and make space for the emotional response**, then establish what the patient wants or is ready to discuss.
distractors: Practical planning matters, but it prematurely closes the immediate emotional discussion.
This may be needed later, but first check whether the patient can engage with further information.
Rephrasing can help understanding, but may bypass the emotional response at this moment.
The patient should be given space to speak for themselves first.
lo: Evaluate the effects of different strategies for breaking bad news.
sources: Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — End of Life.

explanation: The patient has an immediate emotional response that needs space and acknowledgement before more information.

keyClues.quote: has not yet discussed treatment options
explanation: Those options can follow when the patient is ready; their absence does not make an immediate information dump the best response.

keyConcept.summary: The immediate task is to acknowledge and make space for the emotional response, then establish what the patient wants or is ready to discuss.
paragraphs: Silence can provide time to absorb difficult news. An open invitation allows the clinician to discover concerns without assuming what the tears mean. Information can then be paced and understanding checked.

commonTraps: More information is not always the best immediate response.
recogniseNextTime: The cue concerns emotional processing rather than a demonstrated factual misunderstanding.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What might you ask after the pause?
followUpQuestions.answer: “What is going through your mind at the moment?”

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: The immediate task is to acknowledge and make space for the emotional response, then establish what the patient wants or is ready to discuss.

questions.stem: A patient receiving palliative care says their pain is controlled but they cannot sleep because they are worried about how their partner will manage financially. Which next action best addresses the problem described?
options: Arrange a routine medication review as the sole response
Explore the concern and offer help accessing appropriate practical support
Increase analgesia because insomnia usually indicates hidden pain
Provide a sleep-hygiene leaflet before discussing finances
Ask the partner to handle the finances without involving the patient
questions.why: Palliative assessment includes **psychological and social distress**, not only physical symptoms. Explore the worry and agree practical support with the patient.
distractors: A review may be useful but is insufficient for an explicit social concern.
The patient identifies a different concern; reassess symptoms as needed rather than assuming pain.
This may support sleep, but does not address the stated source of distress.
This bypasses the patient’s wishes and may worsen loss of control.
lo: Take a history from a patient with a potentially life threatening illness covering physical, psychological, social and spiritual aspects, focusing in particular on the use of listening skills.
sources: Recommendations | End of life care for adults: service delivery | Guidance | NICE — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng142/chapter/Recommendations
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — End of Life.

Increased renal loss of amino acids
Complete abolition of the brain’s glucose requirement
Reduced demand for amino acids as gluconeogenic substrates
Suppression of all adipose lipolysis

Length-time bias
Attrition bias

No retrospective exposure recall is involved.

No differential missing follow-up is described.

explanation: The measured gain exactly matches the advance in diagnosis, illustrating lead-time bias.

explanation: The serology supports coeliac disease, and normal total IgA makes IgA deficiency less likely to complicate interpretation.
The expected abnormality is villous injury with crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytes, rather than a primarily colonic or gastric lesion.

keyConcept.summary: Coeliac disease can cause villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis, reducing absorptive function.
paragraphs: Small-bowel damage can present through nutrient deficiency as well as gastrointestinal symptoms. Serology and biopsy need appropriate clinical interpretation, including whether the patient has been consuming gluten.

commonTraps: Do not confuse deep transmural inflammation with villous mucosal injury.
recogniseNextTime: The site and mucosal architecture distinguish it from other causes of diarrhoea.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why can iron deficiency be a presenting feature?
followUpQuestions.answer: Damage to proximal small-intestinal mucosa impairs iron absorption.

questions.assessmentObjective: Coeliac disease can cause villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis, reducing absorptive function.

questions.stem: An immune response has prominent IL-17 signalling and recruits neutrophils to an extracellular microbial challenge. Which helper T-cell subset is most closely associated?
options: TH2
Follicular helper T cells
TH1
TH17
Regulatory T cells
questions.why: **TH17 cells** produce IL-17 and support neutrophil-associated defence at barrier sites.
distractors: TH2 responses support eosinophilic and IgE-associated responses.
These provide specialised help to B cells in follicles.
TH1 responses are associated particularly with interferon-gamma and macrophage activation.
These primarily limit immune responses rather than define the IL-17 response.
lo: Identify the key triggers in the development of TH1, TH2 and TH17 responses, and discuss the relevance of these T helper cell subsets in normal and pathological immune responses, with particular reference to inflammatory bowel disease
sources: Interactions between neutrophils and T-helper 17 cells - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10619153/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Gastrointestinal (Malignancy).

explanation: The cytokine provides a more specific clue than inflammation alone.

keyConcept.summary: TH17 cells produce IL-17 and support neutrophil-associated defence at barrier sites.
paragraphs: Helper subsets coordinate different patterns rather than working in isolation. The same tissue can contain several subsets; this question asks which is most directly linked to the described cytokine.

commonTraps: Do not equate every T-helper response with TH1 or TH2.
recogniseNextTime: The cytokine provides a more specific clue than inflammation alone.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which subset is classically linked to interferon-gamma?
followUpQuestions.answer: TH1.

questions.stem: Cardiac muscle cannot normally undergo the sustained tetanic contraction seen in skeletal muscle. Which property is most important?
options: An inability to store calcium in the sarcoplasmic reticulum
A long action potential and refractory period overlapping contraction
A complete absence of calcium entry from extracellular fluid
A requirement for a new motor-neuron impulse for every beat
A lack of actin and myosin overlap
questions.why: The prolonged **refractory period** prevents rapid re-excitation and summation into tetanus.
distractors: Cardiac cells do store and release SR calcium.
Cardiac contraction does depend on extracellular trigger calcium.
Pacemaker activity initiates normal cardiac rhythm without such motor-neuron input.
Cardiac muscle contracts through actin–myosin interaction.
questions.module: Circulation (Peripheral Arterial Disease & Venous Thromboembolic Disease)
lo: Describe the anatomy and physiology of the conducting system of the heart in health, and how this is disrupted in common arrhythmias including ventricular fibrillation and atrial fibrillation
sources: OpenStax: Cardiac muscle and electrical activity — https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-2-cardiac-muscle-and-electrical-activity
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Circulation (Peripheral Arterial Disease & Venous Thromboembolic Disease).

explanation: The question concerns timing of excitability relative to mechanical contraction.

keyConcept.summary: The prolonged refractory period prevents rapid re-excitation and summation into tetanus.
paragraphs: The ventricular action-potential plateau extends refractoriness through much of contraction. This helps preserve alternating contraction and relaxation, allowing filling between beats. It is not due to absence of the normal contractile proteins.

commonTraps: Do not transfer skeletal-muscle summation directly to cardiac muscle.
recogniseNextTime: The question concerns timing of excitability relative to mechanical contraction.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why is relaxation essential for cardiac output?
followUpQuestions.answer: The chambers must refill before the next ejection.

questions.stem: Spirometry shows FEV1 1.4 L, FVC 3.5 L and an FEV1/FVC ratio below the lower limit of normal. Which ventilatory pattern is demonstrated?
options: Obstructive defect
Confirmed restrictive defect
Confirmed mixed obstructive and restrictive defect
Normal spirometry
Isolated gas-transfer impairment
questions.why: A disproportionately reduced FEV1 gives a low FEV1/FVC ratio, supporting **airflow obstruction**.
distractors: Restriction requires reduced total lung capacity; a low ratio supports obstruction.
Restriction cannot be confirmed from these spirometric values alone.
The ratio is explicitly below its lower limit of normal.
Spirometry does not directly measure gas transfer.
lo: Use a peak flow meter and spirometer to diagnose and distinguish between obstructive and restrictive lung disease
sources: Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Introduction).

keyClues.quote: FEV1/FVC ratio below the lower limit of normal
explanation: Disproportionate loss of expiratory flow establishes obstruction.
Spirometry alone does not confirm restriction, which requires reduced total lung capacity, or directly measure gas-transfer capacity.

keyConcept.summary: A disproportionately reduced FEV1 gives a low FEV1/FVC ratio, supporting airflow obstruction.
paragraphs: FVC may fall in several situations, including air trapping. A low FVC alone cannot prove restriction; lung-volume measurement is needed. Spirometry describes a physiological pattern rather than naming the cause.

commonTraps: Do not diagnose a mixed defect without evidence of reduced total lung capacity.
recogniseNextTime: The ratio, interpreted against an appropriate reference, identifies obstruction.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which measurement confirms restriction?
followUpQuestions.answer: Total lung capacity below its lower limit of normal.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.stem: A macrophage responds rapidly to a conserved microbial structure before antigen-specific lymphocyte expansion. Which receptor property best explains this?
options: Recognition requiring prior exposure to the same strain
Binding restricted to peptide presented by MHC class I
Recognition mediated only by secreted IgG
Germline-encoded recognition of shared microbial patterns
Somatic rearrangement generating a unique antibody-binding site
questions.why: Innate **pattern-recognition receptors** recognise conserved microbial features using germline-encoded receptors.
distractors: Innate pattern recognition does not require such prior exposure.
This is characteristic of conventional CD8 T-cell recognition.
Macrophages can recognise microbial patterns without antibody.
This describes adaptive antigen-receptor generation.
lo: Explain the distinction between innate and adaptive immunity and describe the main components of each
sources: Innate Immune Pattern Recognition: A Cell Biological Perspective - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5146691/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Introductory Week.

explanation: Innate receptors recognise shared molecular patterns rather than generating a unique receptor for each new pathogen.
The response does not require prior strain-specific exposure or newly produced IgG.

keyConcept.summary: Innate pattern-recognition receptors recognise conserved microbial features using germline-encoded receptors.
paragraphs: Innate detection helps initiate and shape adaptive immunity. Broad pattern recognition trades fine specificity for rapid coverage of common microbial features; it does not imply that every innate response is identical.

commonTraps: Rapid does not mean unregulated or incapable of influencing memory responses.
recogniseNextTime: The timing and shared target distinguish innate recognition from clonal adaptive responses.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What generates much adaptive receptor diversity?
followUpQuestions.answer: Somatic gene rearrangement in developing lymphocytes.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Innate pattern-recognition receptors recognise conserved microbial features using germline-encoded receptors.

questions.stem: A nitrate relieves angina partly through venodilation. Which immediate haemodynamic change reduces myocardial wall stress?
options: Increased myocardial contractility
Increased venous return and ventricular preload
Reduced venous return and ventricular preload
Increased systemic arteriolar resistance
Increased circulating red-cell mass
questions.why: Venodilation increases venous capacitance, reducing **preload and ventricular wall stress**.
distractors: This increases oxygen demand rather than explaining nitrate relief.
Venodilation increases capacitance and tends to reduce return.
This increases afterload and can increase cardiac work.
Nitrates do not acutely increase red-cell mass.
lo: Explain the mechanism of action of nitrates, beta blockers and calcium channel blockers in the treatment of ischaemic chest pain
sources: Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Ischaemic Heart Disease).

explanation: Follow the effect on blood storage in veins before considering the ventricle.

keyConcept.summary: Venodilation increases venous capacitance, reducing preload and ventricular wall stress.
paragraphs: Lower wall stress can reduce oxygen demand. Nitrates can have additional vascular effects, but the stem asks specifically about the venous mechanism. A reflex increase in heart rate is not their primary therapeutic action.

commonTraps: Do not confuse venodilation with an increase in venous return.
recogniseNextTime: Follow the effect on blood storage in veins before considering the ventricle.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What does venous capacitance mean?
followUpQuestions.answer: The ability of veins to hold blood at a given pressure.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Venodilation increases venous capacitance, reducing preload and ventricular wall stress.

questions.stem: On room air at sea level, an acutely breathless adult has PaO2 6.8 kPa and PaCO2 4.5 kPa. Which pattern is present?
options: Normal gas exchange
Type I respiratory failure
Isolated chronic compensated respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Type II respiratory failure
questions.why: Low PaO2 without hypercapnia indicates **type I respiratory failure**.
distractors: The arterial oxygen tension is substantially reduced.
That would require hypercapnia and appropriate acid–base findings.
This cannot be established from oxygen and CO2 tensions alone.
Type II includes raised arterial CO2, which is not present.
lo: Define type I and type II respiratory failure and describe the common causes
sources: Glossary - Prehospital continuous positive airway pressure for acute respiratory failure: the ACUTE feasibility RCT - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK567215/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Respiratory (Failures).

explanation: The arterial oxygen tension is substantially low on room air.
CO2 is not elevated, supporting type I rather than hypercapnic type II respiratory failure.

keyClues.quote: On room air at sea level
explanation: The environmental context allows interpretation without a high inspired oxygen concentration masking the severity of impaired oxygenation.

keyConcept.summary: Low PaO2 without hypercapnia indicates type I respiratory failure.
paragraphs: Classification identifies a gas-exchange pattern, not a unique disease. Ventilation–perfusion mismatch, shunt and diffusion impairment can contribute to hypoxaemia. The room-air context makes the oxygen value interpretable.

commonTraps: Do not infer a metabolic acid–base disorder without pH and bicarbonate.
recogniseNextTime: CO2 is not raised, separating this pattern from type II failure.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What additional gas finding defines type II failure?
followUpQuestions.answer: Raised arterial CO2 alongside hypoxaemia.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Low PaO2 without hypercapnia indicates type I respiratory failure.

questions.stem: A child has extra chromosome-21 material attached to chromosome 14. A parent carries a balanced rearrangement involving these chromosomes. Which mechanism explains the child’s Down syndrome?
options: Unbalanced Robertsonian translocation
A balanced translocation in the child
Post-zygotic mitotic nondisjunction alone
Uniparental disomy with normal dosage
A chromosome-21 point mutation
questions.why: The child has an **unbalanced translocation** with excess chromosome-21 material; a parent can carry a balanced form without the same phenotype.
distractors: Balanced dosage does not explain the extra chromosome-21 material.
This could cause mosaicism but does not explain the attached chromosome material.
This changes parental origin rather than producing the described excess material.
A point mutation is not an extra chromosome segment.
lo: Identify the ways in which chromosomal abnormalities can occur, and relate this to the epidemiology of and screening for Down’s syndrome
sources: Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Congenital Disorders (Down's Syndrome).

keyClues.quote: extra chromosome-21 material attached to chromosome 14
explanation: Extra chromosome-21 dosage is carried on a structural rearrangement, consistent with an unbalanced Robertsonian translocation.
A balanced parental rearrangement can segregate to an unbalanced gamete; a clinically unaffected carrier can therefore have an affected child.

keyConcept.summary: The child has an unbalanced translocation with excess chromosome-21 material; a parent can carry a balanced form without the same phenotype.
paragraphs: Chromosome number alone can miss clinically important dosage changes. The arrangement and amount of chromosome material matter, and a parental rearrangement has implications for recurrence counselling.

commonTraps: Do not assume a balanced carrier and an affected child have the same chromosome dosage.
recogniseNextTime: The physical rearrangement distinguishes this from free trisomy.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What does “balanced” mean here?
followUpQuestions.answer: No major net gain or loss of the relevant chromosomal material.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: The child has an unbalanced translocation with excess chromosome-21 material; a parent can carry a balanced form without the same phenotype.

questions.stem: Six days after a large myocardial infarction, a patient suddenly collapses with pulseless electrical activity and raised jugular venous pressure. Bedside ultrasound shows a new large pericardial collection. Which complication is most likely?
options: Recurrent uncomplicated pericarditis
Left ventricular aneurysm
Ventricular septal rupture
Papillary muscle rupture
Left ventricular free-wall rupture
questions.why: Infarcted myocardium can rupture, causing **haemopericardium and tamponade**. The new pericardial collection is decisive.
distractors: Inflammation alone is a poorer explanation for sudden collapse with this post-infarct pattern.
This develops as a later structural complication and does not best explain acute tamponade.
This causes a new septal shunt, not the described pericardial collection.
This produces acute mitral regurgitation and pulmonary oedema rather than haemopericardium.
lo: Describe the typical pathological changes in myocardial infarction at both macroscopic and microscopic levels over time
sources: AHA Scientific Statement: Mechanical Complications of Acute Myocardial Infarction A Scientific Statement from the American Heart Association - PMC — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9364424/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Ischaemic Heart Disease).

keyClues.quote: Six days after a large myocardial infarction
explanation: Macrophage clearance weakens infarcted tissue before a mature scar forms, creating a window for mechanical rupture.

keyClues.quote: pulseless electrical activity and raised jugular venous pressure
explanation: This combination suggests impaired cardiac filling or output despite organised electrical activity, compatible with tamponade.
Blood entering the pericardium after free-wall rupture explains tamponade. Septal or papillary muscle rupture causes different internal mechanical defects.

keyConcept.summary: Infarcted myocardium can rupture, causing haemopericardium and tamponade
paragraphs: Removal of dead tissue precedes a strong collagen scar, creating a vulnerable period after infarction. Tamponade impairs filling despite ongoing electrical activity. This is a recognition question, not a reason to delay resuscitation.

commonTraps: A post-MI collapse has several causes; do not ignore the ultrasound finding.
recogniseNextTime: The location of the fluid distinguishes free-wall rupture from intracardiac mechanical complications.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What valve lesion follows papillary muscle rupture?
followUpQuestions.answer: Acute severe mitral regurgitation.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Infarcted myocardium can rupture, causing haemopericardium and tamponade

questions.stem: A cell acquires loss-of-function changes in both copies of a gene that normally restrains proliferation. Which class of gene is most consistent?
options: An overexpressed oncogenic transcription factor
Proto-oncogene activated by increased signalling
Tumour-suppressor gene
Constitutively activated growth-factor receptor
An activated telomerase promoter
questions.why: Loss of a **tumour suppressor** removes a restraint on cell growth or survival.
distractors: This also increases growth-promoting activity.
That typically contributes through gain of function rather than the loss described.
This is a growth-promoting gain-of-function example.
This promotes continued replication rather than removing the stated brake.
lo: Explain how gene mutations in oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes may lead to the development of malignancy
sources: Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Malignancies (Breast Cancer).

explanation: Loss of both functional copies is the classic two-hit pattern for many tumour-suppressor genes, rather than activation of an oncogene.
The normal gene is a brake on growth; losing its function removes that restraint.

keyConcept.summary: Loss of a tumour suppressor removes a restraint on cell growth or survival.
paragraphs: Many tumour-suppressor pathways follow a two-hit pattern, but not every cancer gene behaves identically. Gene class describes a functional role; the overall malignant phenotype usually requires multiple cooperating changes.

commonTraps: Do not call every cancer-associated mutation an activated oncogene.
recogniseNextTime: The normal function and direction of change distinguish the gene class.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What change typically activates a proto-oncogene?
followUpQuestions.answer: A gain-of-function change or inappropriate overexpression.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Loss of a tumour suppressor removes a restraint on cell growth or survival.

questions.stem: A superficial vein ascends along the medial side of the lower limb and joins the femoral vein in the groin. Which vessel is described?
options: Popliteal vein
Small saphenous vein
Anterior tibial vein
Great saphenous vein
External iliac vein
questions.why: The **great saphenous vein** follows the medial lower limb and enters the femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction.
distractors: This is a deep vein behind the knee rather than the described superficial vessel.
This usually ascends posteriorly in the calf and drains into the popliteal vein.
This is a deep vein accompanying the anterior tibial artery.
This lies proximally above the inguinal ligament, not along the medial leg.
questions.module: Circulation (Peripheral Arterial Disease & Venous Thromboembolic Disease)
lo: Describe in outline the structure of the peripheral vascular system, relating this to the function of the cardiac and muscle pumps
sources: Anatomy, Bony Pelvis and Lower Limb: Saphenous Nerve, Artery, and Vein - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK541045/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Circulation (Peripheral Arterial Disease & Venous Thromboembolic Disease).

explanation: This excludes the deep veins listed as the described vessel.

keyClues.quote: medial side of the lower limb and joins the femoral vein
explanation: The course and saphenofemoral junction identify the great saphenous vein; the small saphenous usually drains into the popliteal vein.

keyConcept.summary: The great saphenous vein follows the medial lower limb and enters the femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction.
paragraphs: Superficial and deep veins communicate through perforators. Valves support directed return, while valve dysfunction can contribute to varicosities. Knowing the course and connection is more useful than memorising a vessel name alone.

commonTraps: Do not swap the great and small saphenous drainage sites.
recogniseNextTime: The tissue plane and drainage site distinguish superficial from deep vessels.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Where does the small saphenous vein usually drain?
followUpQuestions.answer: Into the popliteal vein.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.stem: A haemoglobin variant polymerises more readily when deoxygenated, distorting erythrocytes and contributing to vaso-occlusion. Which change causes classical sickle haemoglobin?
options: A complete absence of alpha-globin synthesis
Loss of the red-cell membrane protein spectrin
Deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Reduced beta-globin production without the HbS substitution
A glutamate-to-valine substitution in beta globin
questions.why: HbS contains a **beta-globin amino-acid substitution** that promotes polymerisation in the deoxygenated state.
distractors: This describes severe alpha-thalassaemia rather than HbS.
This causes a membrane disorder rather than the HbS structural variant.
This affects oxidative defence, not globin sequence.
This describes beta-thalassaemia.
lo: Describe the genetic basis of the common haemoglobinopathies, including alpha and beta thalassaemia and sickle cell disease
sources: Sickle Cell Disease - GeneReviews® - NCBI Bookshelf — https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1377/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Anaemia.

explanation: Deoxygenation-dependent polymerisation is the central property of HbS, produced by the beta-globin glutamate-to-valine substitution.
Sickling-related loss of deformability explains vascular obstruction; membrane spectrin or G6PD defects cause haemolysis through different mechanisms.

keyConcept.summary: HbS contains a beta-globin amino-acid substitution that promotes polymerisation in the deoxygenated state.
paragraphs: Sickle cell disease and thalassaemia both involve haemoglobin but through different molecular mechanisms: altered structure versus reduced chain synthesis. Genotype influences phenotype, and the two can coexist.

commonTraps: Do not use “reduced haemoglobin production” as the specific HbS mechanism.
recogniseNextTime: The oxygen-dependent structural behaviour identifies HbS rather than a globin-production defect.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What environmental change favours HbS polymerisation?
followUpQuestions.answer: Deoxygenation.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.stem: A service wants to reduce recurrent cardiovascular events in patients with established coronary disease. Which intervention is secondary prevention in this context?
options: Blood-pressure screening in adults without known cardiovascular disease
Reducing dietary salt in a school-meal programme
Smoking-prevention education before tobacco use begins
Statin treatment after a documented myocardial infarction
Screening asymptomatic relatives for cardiovascular risk factors
questions.why: Treatment after established coronary disease aims to prevent **further events**, making it secondary prevention in cardiovascular practice.
distractors: This is primary prevention in the stated context.
This is population-level primary prevention.
This is prevention before disease develops.
This is primary prevention for relatives without established disease.
lo: Distinguish between primary and secondary prevention, giving examples of each
sources: Quality statement 5: Secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease | Cardiovascular risk assessment and lipid modification | Quality standards | NICE — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/qs100/chapter/Quality-statement-5-Secondary-prevention-of-cardiovascular-disease
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Ischaemic Heart Disease).

explanation: The patient already has the disease; prevention level depends on that starting point.

keyConcept.summary: Treatment after established coronary disease aims to prevent further events, making it secondary prevention in cardiovascular practice.
paragraphs: The same drug can be used for primary or secondary prevention in different people. Terminology also varies by context: in screening theory, secondary prevention often refers to early disease detection. Here the cardiovascular-event context is explicit.

commonTraps: Do not assign prevention level from the drug name alone.
recogniseNextTime: The patient already has the disease; prevention level depends on that starting point.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Can a statin also be used in primary prevention?
followUpQuestions.answer: Yes, in someone without established cardiovascular disease when indicated.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.stem: After equal intravenous doses of two drugs, the initial equilibrated plasma concentration of X is much lower than that of Y. Assuming negligible elimination during this comparison, what does this suggest?
options: X has a smaller apparent volume of distribution
X has a larger apparent volume of distribution
X must have a shorter elimination half-life
X necessarily has a higher renal clearance
X has a higher oral bioavailability
questions.why: **Vd = amount of drug in the body / plasma concentration**. With equal amounts, lower plasma concentration indicates larger apparent Vd.
distractors: For the same amount, a lower concentration implies a larger Vd.
Half-life depends on both distribution volume and clearance.
Elimination is excluded from the comparison and Vd does not specify clearance.
Both doses were intravenous, so oral absorption is irrelevant.
lo: Calculate drug dilutions and doses using volumes of distribution and drug clearances to obtain safe and effective concentrations of drugs in plasma
sources: Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Introductory Week.

explanation: The delivered dose is controlled and there is no oral absorption comparison.

keyClues.quote: plasma concentration of X is much lower
explanation: Apparent volume of distribution equals amount of drug in the body divided by plasma concentration: a lower concentration at the same amount means a larger apparent volume.
Clearance differences are excluded as the explanation during this comparison, and half-life cannot be inferred from concentration alone.

keyConcept.summary: Vd = amount of drug in the body / plasma concentration
paragraphs: Apparent Vd is a mathematical volume, not a measured anatomical compartment. Extensive tissue binding can produce values greater than total body volume because plasma contains only a small fraction of the total drug.

commonTraps: Do not infer elimination rate from distribution volume alone.
recogniseNextTime: This isolates distribution from loss of drug from the body.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which dose is directly influenced by Vd?
followUpQuestions.answer: The loading dose for a chosen target concentration.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Vd = amount of drug in the body / plasma concentration

questions.stem: A 28-year-old has recurrent episodes of headache, sweating and palpitations with marked blood-pressure surges. Blood pressure is lower between episodes. Which secondary cause is most likely?
options: Primary hyperaldosteronism
Phaeochromocytoma
Coarctation of the aorta
Renal artery stenosis
Cushing syndrome
questions.why: Episodic catecholamine release from a **phaeochromocytoma** can produce this combination of symptoms and pressure surges.
distractors: This can cause sustained hypertension and hypokalaemia but does not best explain the paroxysmal adrenergic pattern.
This would suggest arm–leg pressure and pulse differences rather than adrenergic attacks.
This activates the renin–angiotensin system but is less characteristic of these episodic symptoms.
This causes a different pattern of systemic features and usually more sustained hypertension.
lo: Identify the risk factors predisposing to high blood pressure, including the causes of secondary hypertension
sources: Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Circulation (Hypertension).

explanation: The symptom cluster fits episodic catecholamine excess.
Paroxysms with lower pressure between episodes strengthen the case for phaeochromocytoma over the more sustained hypertension typical of the other listed causes.

keyConcept.summary: Episodic catecholamine release from a phaeochromocytoma can produce this combination of symptoms and pressure surges.
paragraphs: Secondary hypertension should be considered when age, severity or associated features are atypical. The clinical pattern raises suspicion but is not diagnostic without appropriate biochemical and anatomical assessment.

commonTraps: A headache in any hypertensive patient is not sufficient to identify this tumour.
recogniseNextTime: Paroxysmal symptoms are more informative than hypertension alone.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which broad class of mediators is released?
followUpQuestions.answer: Catecholamines.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: Episodic catecholamine release from a phaeochromocytoma can produce this combination of symptoms and pressure surges.

questions.stem: A doctor discovers that their signed note incorrectly records a normal neurological examination that was not performed. The patient remains on the ward. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Wait until the next routine ward round before mentioning the error
Delete the original entry and replace it with a normal examination after seeing the patient
Add the examination to the discharge summary only
Ask a colleague to perform the examination without correcting the note
Make a dated correction preserving the original entry and inform the team so the patient can be reassessed
questions.why: The response should combine **transparent correction and prompt clinical communication**, with reassessment of any unmet need.
distractors: This leaves the team relying on inaccurate information in the meantime.
This obscures what was recorded and when.
A later summary does not correct the immediate clinical record.
Reassessment alone leaves a misleading record.
lo: Be familiar with the principles of good medical practice and the reasoning behind them as defined by the GMC
sources: Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Introductory Week.

explanation: The record contains a factual error; obtaining an examination later cannot make the original entry accurate.
The team can act now to reassess the patient. A traceable correction and communication address both record integrity and current clinical care.

keyConcept.summary: The response should combine transparent correction and prompt clinical communication, with reassessment of any unmet need.
paragraphs: An accurate audit trail helps others understand what was known at each stage. Correcting documentation and addressing patient safety are complementary tasks. Follow local reporting and candour processes where applicable.

commonTraps: Do not erase the history of an error to make the record look cleaner.
recogniseNextTime: The problem is a false record of an assessment, not merely a typographical error.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why inform the clinical team as well as amend the note?
followUpQuestions.answer: They may already be making decisions based on the incorrect information.

provenance.adaptation: Rewritten and expanded for this draft

questions.assessmentObjective: The response should combine transparent correction and prompt clinical communication, with reassessment of any unmet need.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient has limited English and is discussing an important non-urgent screening decision. Their adult relative offers to interpret. What is the best next arrangement?
options: Postpone discussion indefinitely until the patient learns more English
Give an English leaflet and proceed if the patient nods
Use the relative by default because they know the patient well
Ask the relative to choose the screening option
Offer a professional interpreter and speak directly to the patient
questions.why: Offer **professional interpretation** so the patient can understand, ask questions and make their own decision.
distractors: This creates an avoidable barrier to informed care.
Nodding does not establish adequate understanding.
This may affect accuracy, privacy and the patient’s freedom to express concerns.
The decision belongs to the patient, not the interpreter.
lo: Discuss the factors which promote or inhibit effective communication with patients and colleagues
sources: NHS England » Interpreting and translation in primary care — https://www.england.nhs.uk/interpreting/
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Start in Life.

explanation: There is time to arrange reliable communication so consent can be informed.

questions.stem: Left ventricular pressure has just fallen below aortic pressure, but remains above left atrial pressure. Which valve state is expected during this phase?

Aortic closed and mitral open
Aortic partly open and mitral open
Aortic open and mitral open
Aortic closed and mitral closed
questions.why: This is **isovolumetric relaxation**: the aortic valve has closed, but the mitral valve has not yet opened.
distractors: The aortic valve closes when ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure.
The mitral valve opens only once ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.
The pressure relations favour closure of both valves, not filling.
Normal pressure-driven valve operation does not produce this state here.

paragraphs: Valve movement follows pressure gradients. During the interval with both valves closed, ventricular pressure changes while volume is approximately constant. Use the gradients rather than memorising valve states in isolation.

commonTraps: Do not equate ventricular relaxation with immediate ventricular filling.
recogniseNextTime: Ventricular pressure is still too high for passive inflow from the atrium.

Both increase
Both decrease

questions.stem: A jaundiced patient has pale stools and a much larger rise in ALP and GGT than in ALT. Which biochemical pattern is most likely?

Predominantly hepatocellular injury
Isolated bone disease
Cholestatic injury or obstruction

distractors: This mainly increases unconjugated bilirubin and does not best explain raised cholestatic enzymes with pale stools.

Bone can raise ALP, but the GGT and biliary symptoms support a hepatic source.
This gives isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia rather than the stated enzyme pattern.

keyClues.quote: much larger rise in ALP and GGT than in ALT
explanation: A disproportionate ALP/GGT rise is cholestatic. GGT supports a hepatobiliary source of ALP rather than isolated bone disease.

keyConcept.summary: A disproportionate ALP and GGT rise with pale stools supports cholestasis.

Biguanide
GLP-1 receptor agonist
SGLT2 inhibitor

This acts on proximal tubular glucose transport.

explanation: The binding site discriminates from other medicines that can also affect insulin secretion indirectly.

A direct measurement of skeletal-muscle mass
Distribution of central adiposity
A definitive diagnosis of insulin resistance
A measurement of resting metabolic rate

This requires a different assessment.

questions.stem: A treatment trial measures the primary outcome in 65% of the intervention group and 95% of controls. Missingness is associated with adverse effects and poorer prognosis. What is the main concern?
options: Ecological fallacy
Recall bias
Bias due to missing outcome data
Length-time bias
Lead-time bias
questions.why: **Differential, prognosis-related missing outcomes** can distort the treatment comparison.
distractors: The analysis is not inferring individual effects from group-level associations.
The problem is absent outcomes, not differential memory.
No screening selection of slower disease is described.
No earlier diagnosis is changing the survival clock.
lo: Describe challenges to internal validity for a randomised controlled trial
sources: Cochrane Handbook: Risk of bias in a randomised trial — https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-08
Curriculum: BM4 Year 1 learning outcomes — Cardiac Function (Heart Failure).

keyClues.quote: 65% of the intervention group and 95% of controls
explanation: Outcome completeness differs between the treatment groups; the analysed sample may no longer preserve the original comparison.

keyClues.quote: Missingness is associated with adverse effects and poorer prognosis
explanation: The missing outcomes are related to likely results. This is informative attrition, not an error in remembering past exposure or a screening-related survival artefact.

keyConcept.summary: Differential, prognosis-related missing outcomes can distort the treatment comparison.
paragraphs: Stopping a drug and losing outcome follow-up are not the same event. Intention-to-treat principles do not magically supply unmeasured outcomes; missing-data assumptions and sensitivity analyses still matter.

commonTraps: Do not claim attrition bias merely because patients discontinue medication if their outcomes remain measured.

questions.stem: A renal biopsy in a patient with longstanding hypertension shows homogeneous pink thickening of arteriolar walls with luminal narrowing. Which lesion best fits?

Medial calcific sclerosis
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis
Atherosclerosis
Fibrinoid necrosis
questions.why: **Hyaline arteriolosclerosis** is associated with chronic hypertension and diabetes and narrows small-vessel lumina.
distractors: This produces concentric laminated “onion-skin” thickening rather than homogeneous hyaline material.
This involves calcification of muscular arterial media rather than hyaline arteriolar thickening.
This principally affects larger arteries with intimal plaques, not this arteriolar lesion.
This is destructive acute vascular injury rather than the chronic homogeneous wall change.

keyClues.quote: homogeneous pink thickening of arteriolar walls
explanation: Hyaline material in small arterial walls is the central morphological clue. Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis instead gives concentric onion-skin layering.

Diffusion decreases as barrier thickness increases

Barrier properties also influence diffusion.

Hydrogen-ion secretion by gastric parietal cells
Excretion of filtered bicarbonate
Release of bicarbonate from pancreatic ducts
Ammonium excretion and generation of new bicarbonate

questions.stem: A hypothetical drug is mainly cleared by hepatic metabolism. Severe liver dysfunction reduces its clearance while the intravenous maintenance dose rate stays unchanged. Under linear kinetics, what is expected at steady state?

No concentration change because intravenous drugs bypass the liver
A necessarily shorter elimination half-life
A higher plasma drug concentration
A necessarily smaller volume of distribution

distractors: Reduced clearance at the same input increases exposure.
